properties.name: LESSON: a normaliser's "absent means the old default" rule, applied to a FRESH write, smuggled `author` into a first-ever `approver` — and the order-independence test passed because both orders were wrong the same way; only the write-once test caught it
properties.statement:
While fixing AUTHORED_BY (roles as a set), the writer called the legacy normaliser on whatever it found for the (node, contributor) pair — including an EMPTY map when no edge existed. The normaliser's rule "no `role` recorded means `author`" is correct for a stored legacy edge (the old schema default) and WRONG for a map that is empty because nothing was ever written: the first `approver` write came out as [author, approver].

TWO TESTS HAD ALREADY PASSED OVER THIS. `approving_what_you_authored_keeps_both_roles` wrote author first, so the phantom coincided with the truth. `the_roles_are_a_set_in_canonical_order_whatever_the_write_order` compared the two orders to EACH OTHER — both produced [author, approver], both wrongly, and the equality held. The test that failed was the smallest one: write `approver` twice, expect exactly [approver].

THE RULES:
1. A default belongs to STORED data with a history, never to a value that is absent because it was never written. Normalise what you found; do not normalise nothing.
2. An order-independence test proves symmetry, not correctness. Pair it with a single-write test that pins the exact expected value, or it will bless two identical mistakes.
3. This is the schema-defaults finding again (`fact:the-schema-declares-81-defaults-and-nothing-reads-them`, BL-198): "absent" and "somebody said the default" look the same in the store, and any code that resolves absence to a default is deciding, silently, which one it was.
